sentiment.instructions: Read the text and decide which sentiment it expresses overall. Consider the text as a whole rather than individual words, and take irony, sarcasm and negation into account.

positive.description: The text as a whole conveys approval, praise, satisfaction, enthusiasm, gratitude, affection or another favorable stance. A text that mentions some drawbacks still counts as positive if the favorable stance clearly dominates.
examples: Not even 20 pages into Paper Towns and the book centers around the night of May 5th. I know its gonna be a good one now!

neutral.description: The text conveys no clear sentiment. This includes purely factual statements, questions, announcements and texts whose positive and negative parts roughly balance each other.
examples: I may be sleep deprived but I promise you that some kid at Dunkin today looked like a sprout.

negative.description: The text as a whole conveys criticism, complaint, anger, sadness, fear, disgust, disappointment or another unfavorable stance. A text that mentions some good points still counts as negative if the unfavorable stance clearly dominates.
examples: The tragedy of only thinking up hilarious tweets for the Summer Olympics now is that in four years there may be no place for them.
